text: I struggle to believe at an intuitive level that autonomous R&D is so ingenious. I have been monitoring a few side projects: In all of these cases, the model's judgment is just very poor in a basic way. For example: I judged an Apart hackathon last weekend and reviewed eight papers, all of which scored between 60% and 95% on Pangram. Predictably, the papers were often very similar to each other, and kind of methodologically incomplete in a vague but similar way, where they seem to overlook the most straightforward analysis. Maybe the important exception is certain hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops. For example, I improved the SOTA on "listing all legal Scrabble moves" by 10x just by prompting Astra over and over to try harder, to aim for <specific performance level>, to "systematically try every method in the literature that seems kind of related," etc. But even in that case, two big leaps were when I said that it should take into account the fact that you can measure across a game rather than per random position, and suggesting that it try to design algorithms for three different cases based on the number of blank tiles left in the bag (which cause the number of moves to explode). There is also the fact that Astra at least (and presumably Claude) tends to write reports that are extremely difficult to understand and some kind of Q&A interrogation is often needed to figure out what it actually did and what the key results are. Maybe there's a temptation to just say "whatever" and let it rip. I agree with you. AIs are good when pointed in the right direction (the key sources to refer to, the best metric to hill-climb, the parts of the story a human would find most surprising), but a human often still has to point them in the right direction first. While it's nice that we Humans are still useful, it's sort of weird that this shepherding is still necessary. But IMO it bears out empirically, not just on vibes/anecdotes.
